newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Shell confident of securing Kudu gas customers.
newsitem.headline: Shell confident of securing Kudu gas customers.

text.p: Shell Exploration and Production Namibia BV remains confident of securing anchor clients in South Africa to take up product from its Kudu gas field in Namibia, managing director Ger Kegge said.
He told the African Upstream conference that the Namibian market would be too small for the planned gas field and exports to South Africa would be important to ensure viability.
These could include gas for a new power station at Saldanha Bay and the development of mineral beneficiation and other industries using gas in the Northern and Western Cape.
He said that although negotiations had already started with potential clients, no final deals could be expected until drilling and evaluation at the Kudu-4 well had been completed.
"We can only go full speed ahead after we have the necessary information from Kudu 4," Kegge told Reuters. This was likely to be in the second quarter of next year.
"By then we should have updated our plans and then we should have an idea of the costs and then we will be able to go out full steam."

Kegge told the conference that as a contigency against a possible delay in the development of a large gas market, the Kudu partnership was presently investigating how a fast track but smaller project could be viable.
"The impatience of Namibia to ensure a secure source of electricity also plays an important role."

The development of a gas market in South Africa has often been dismissed because of its abundance of cheap coal, but Kegge said he was confident that gas could compete with coal in some parts of Southern Africa.

On allegations that initial prices quoted for gas were too high, he said there had been initial uncertainties about prices "because we had not done all our homework" and a clearer picture would emerge next year.
He was confident that Shell would be able to offer competitive prices.

Shell has promoted gas imports as an ideal way in which South Africa could deal with its trade imbalance with Namibia, but Kegge denied that Shell was trying to exert political pressure on South Africa to develop anchor clients.
He said long-term contracts would be involved.
"(With) arm-twisting and shotgun weddings you don't get anywhere. We are not banking on any political pressure.
"We want to convince people that gas has some value and we can try to add value to the gas," Kegge said.
